q-73625:
First, we need to convert $D$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 8 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 8 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 8 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $D$ has $3$ pivots, and therefore the number of pivot columns is $3.$

q-130256:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
D(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})=aD({y}_{1})+bD({y}_{2})
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

Let's check each case in turn.

- The first operator is **not** linear. To see why, we first evaluate the left-hand side of the linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{1}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}^{2}{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+{b}^{2}{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+ab({y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x})\end{aligned}
$$

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because

$$
\begin{aligned}a{D}_{1}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{1}({y}_{2}) & =a[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+a{y}_{1}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+b{y}_{2}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The second operator is indeed linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{2}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & =2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})-x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =2a\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2b\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-ax\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}-bx\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =a[2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{D}_{2}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{2}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- The third operator is also linear. To see this, we check the above linearity condition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{3}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2})+2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(a{y}_{1}+b{y}_{2}) \\  & =a{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+b{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2ax\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}+2bx\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x} \\  & =a[{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{1}}{\text{d}x}]+b[{x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2x\frac{\text{d}{y}_{2}}{\text{d}x}] \\  & =a{D}_{3}({y}_{1})+b{D}_{3}({y}_{2})\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

q-64900:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L({y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}) & =L({y}_{1})+2L({y}_{2}) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x+2\cdot ({sin}^{2}⁡x+4) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x+2{sin}^{2}⁡x+8 \\  & =2({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)+8 \\  & =2+8 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

q-79606:
For any linear differential operator,

$$
L(a{y}_{1}(x)+b{y}_{2}(x))=aL({y}_{1}(x))+bL({y}_{2}(x))
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. 

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L({y}_{1}-3{y}_{2}) & =L({y}_{1})-3L({y}_{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}+3x+5-3(x+2) \\  & ={x}^{2}+3x+5-3x-6 \\  & ={x}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To create a schematic of the Cartesian product, we create a table and list the elements of the first set $A$ in a row across the top and the elements of the second set $B$ in a column down the left side.

q-105862:
For any two finite sets $A$ and $B,$ the cardinality of $A\times B$ is

$$
|A\times B|=|A|\cdot |B|.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|M\times M| & =|M|\cdot |M| \\  & =10\cdot 10 \\  & =100.\end{aligned}
$$

q-105861:
For any two finite sets $M$ and $N,$ the cardinality of $M\times N$ is

$$
|M\times N|=|M|\cdot |N|.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|M\times N| & =|M|\cdot |N| \\  & =7\cdot 6 \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$

q-332642:
To find the complementary solution, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+6{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable since we can write it as

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}=-6{y}_{c}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}=-6
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int -6\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\text{d}{y}_{c} & =\int -6\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|{y}_{c}| & =-6x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we make ${y}_{c}$ the subject by exponentiating both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}|{y}_{c}| & ={e}^{-6x+C} \\  & ={e}^{-6x}{e}^{C} \\  & =K{e}^{-6x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}.$ 

Finally, we can drop the absolute value by allowing the arbitrary constant to be either positive or negative, i.e., setting $A=\pm K.$  Therefore, the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-6x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

q-332727:
To find the complementary solution, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Notice that this differential equation is separable since we can write it as

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}=5{y}_{c}.
$$

Therefore, we separate the variables as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}=5
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\frac{\text{d}{y}_{c}}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}_{c}}\,\text{d}{y}_{c} & =\int 5\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|{y}_{c}| & =5x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we make ${y}_{c}$ the subject by exponentiating both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}|{y}_{c}| & ={e}^{5x+C} \\  & ={e}^{5x}{e}^{C} \\  & =K{e}^{5x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}.$ 

Finally, we can drop the absolute value by allowing the arbitrary constant to be either positive or negative, i.e., setting $A=\pm K.$  Therefore, the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

q-332325:
The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is a polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also a polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.,

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma 
$$

where $\alpha ,$ $\beta ,$ and $\gamma $ are constants to be determined. 

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=2\alpha x+\beta .
$$

To find the values of $\alpha ,$ $\beta $ and $\gamma ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
2(2\alpha x+\beta )+2(\alpha {x}^{2}+\beta x+\gamma )={x}^{2}-2
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
2\alpha {x}^{2}+(4\alpha +2\beta )x+(2\beta +2\gamma )={x}^{2}-2.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\alpha =1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,{x}^{2}) \\ 4\alpha +2\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,x) \\ 2\beta +2\gamma =-2\, & (\text{equating the constants})\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{2},\beta =-1,\gamma =0.$

Therefore, the particular integral ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-x.
$$
